c.tagline: Brazil's steamy geographic heart, where the Cerrado, Amazon, and Pantanal collide.

card: Widely accepted in hotels, malls, and mid-range/upscale restaurants in the center and Goiabeiras; carry cash for markets, street food, small bars, and rural Pantanal/Chapada lodges where card machines are unreliable.

taxi.color: White, with rooftop taxi sign and red municipal plate
taxi.fare: Flag drop R$6.00 plus ~R$4.30/km (Bandeira 1), rising to R$6.00/km at night/Bandeira 2
taxi.fareNote: A short 3-5 km ride across downtown runs roughly $5-9; agree on or confirm the meter is running, especially from the airport or bus terminal.

emergency.note: 193 covers fire and rescue (Corpo de Bombeiros). Operators typically speak only Portuguese, so having a local contact or translation app ready helps in an emergency.

walk: The historic center around Praça da República is compact and walkable, but Cuiabá's brutal heat (often 95°F+) and sprawling newer districts (Goiabeiras, CPA, Araés) make walking between neighborhoods impractical; most visitors pair short walks downtown with taxis or rideshare for everything else.

safety.safety: Moderate, uneven safety - daytime in the center, CPA, and Jardim das Américas is generally fine with normal urban precautions, but conditions deteriorate after dark and in outlying bairros.
safety.crime: Notable concern over robbery and property crime; nighttime walking safety is rated low. Stick to busy, well-lit streets after dark, keep valuables out of sight, use registered taxis or Uber/99 rather than walking or riding late buses at night, and avoid Pedregal and Jardim Vitória, which locals flag as higher-crime areas.

hood_landmark.Araés: Base Aérea de Cuiabá (former city airfield)

avoid.reason: Avoid peripheral low-income neighborhoods such as Pedra 90 and the deserted downtown/old center after dark due to street robbery risk.
Phone and bag snatching happens in the center and at bus stops; keep valuables hidden and use ride-hailing apps at night.

hood_desc: Cuiabá's colonial-era core, anchored by Praça da República where the Catedral Basílica do Senhor Bom Jesus, the Palácio da Instrução, and the Museu Rondon cluster around leafy gardens; narrow streets radiate out with government offices, budget hotels, and everyday capital-city bustle.

The old river port on the Rio Cuiabá, once the 18th-century gold-rush gateway to Mato Grosso, now home to the Mercado do Porto food stalls, the Museu do Rio Cuiabá, and riverside walkways where fishing boats still tie up at dusk.

A leafy, well-off swath of wide avenues and gated condos surrounding Parque Mãe Bonifácia's cerrado trails; widely cited as the city's safest, quietest base, popular with business travelers visiting the nearby state government complex.
A fast-growing commercial district built around Goiabeiras Shopping and the UFMT university campus, packed with chain hotels, malls, and restaurants aimed at business and transit travelers.

A central, traffic-heavy neighborhood that grew up around Cuiabá's old city airfield; after dark its side streets fill with botecos, live-music bars, and late-night kitchens, making it the city's go-to strip for a night out.

water.note: Tap water is treated but most visitors and many locals stick to filtered or bottled water.

transit.sys: Consórcio Cuiabá municipal bus network (regulated by ARSEC)
transit.hours: Roughly 5:00am-11:00pm on most lines; service is sparse late at night
transit.pay: Cash or the rechargeable Cuiabá Card (bilhete único) tapped on boarding; flat fare is R$4.60 (~$0.90) per ride
transit.map: No robust official real-time app; Moovit is the most commonly used third-party tool for route planning
transit.note: Buses can be crowded and infrequent off-peak; not recommended for tourists after dark. Ride-hailing (Uber/99) is faster, cheap, and generally the safer choice for visitors.

transport.air: Marechal Rondon International Airport (CGB), ~8km/20-40 min from downtown in neighboring Várzea Grande, with frequent domestic flights from São Paulo, Brasília, Rio de Janeiro, and other Brazilian hubs; no scheduled direct international flights.
transport.train: None - Brazil has no functioning long-distance passenger rail service reaching Cuiabá.
transport.bus: Rodoviária de Cuiabá (long-distance terminal) links to Campo Grande, São Paulo, Brasília, and other regional cities; overland journeys are long (24+ hours to São Paulo).
transport.ferry: None scheduled - Cuiabá is inland; recreational river/flotel trips run into the Pantanal but aren't a transit option.
transport.car: Reachable via the BR-364 and BR-163 highways; a rental car helps for day trips to Chapada dos Guimarães and the Transpantaneira but isn't needed within the compact center.

airport.name: Marechal Rondon International Airport
airport.distance: ~8 km (5 mi) / 20-40 minutes from downtown, located in Várzea Grande
airport.transport: Airport taxis and Uber/99 both operate curbside; a taxi downtown runs roughly $10-18 depending on traffic; public buses connect the airport to the city bus terminal as the cheapest but slowest option

net.m: Good 4G coverage across the city center and main corridors; signal weakens quickly once outside town toward the Pantanal or Chapada dos Guimarães
net.w: Free wifi is common in hotels, cafes, malls (Goiabeiras Shopping, Shopping Pantanal), and the airport; less reliable at budget guesthouses
net.gb: About $12-30/month for a prepaid plan with 20-50GB, or from around $5 for a short-term tourist eSIM bundle
net.fwn: Airport, shopping malls, and most mid-range/upscale hotels; wifi in the historic center's public squares is inconsistent
net.ap: A local SIM or eSIM (TIM or Claro) is advisable if traveling independently or heading toward the Pantanal/Chapada, since maps and translation apps are essential

tip.s: A 10% service charge ('taxa de serviço') is often already added to restaurant bills; if not included, leaving 10% is customary and appreciated but not obligatory.
tip.r: Round up or leave small change for taxi drivers, bartenders, and hotel staff; Pantanal/Chapada tour guides are commonly tipped around $5-10 per day per person.
